case_analysis.focal_point: Whether FIFRA expressly preempts a Missouri common-law failure-to-warn verdict that would require Monsanto to add (or effectively add) a cancer warning to a Roundup label when EPA has determined such a warning is not required and label changes cannot be made without EPA approval.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), 7 U.S.C. § 136 et seq., especially 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b) (state "requirements" for labeling/packaging that are "in addition to or different from" federal requirements), and the EPA labeling-approval scheme implemented through FIFRA regulations.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Monsanto argues that the Missouri failure-to-warn judgment is preempted because (1) FIFRA § 136v(b) bars any state-law "requirement" that would impose labeling duties different from or in addition to EPA-approved labeling requirements, and tort verdicts function as such requirements; (2) EPA has repeatedly considered cancer-warning language for glyphosate and determined it is not required (and in some contexts would be misleading), so the state verdict conflicts with and adds to the federal labeling determination; and (3) because Monsanto cannot unilaterally add the warning without prior EPA approval, compliance with the state-law duty would be impossible (or would force a federally noncompliant label), making the claim preempted under both FIFRA’s express preemption and conflict/impossibility principles as applied to federally controlled labels.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Durnell argues that his claim is not preempted because (1) FIFRA sets a federal floor and generally permits states to regulate pesticide use and to provide traditional tort remedies, so long as they parallel federal misbranding duties (e.g., the duty not to sell a product with inadequate warnings); (2) EPA registration and labeling approval should not be treated as a definitive federal determination that additional warnings are forbidden, particularly where state law seeks to vindicate a general duty to warn rather than dictate specific label text; (3) Monsanto could have pursued EPA approval for stronger warnings and cannot invoke preemption based on an asserted inability to add language it never successfully sought to add (or that EPA might have allowed under other formulations), so there is no true impossibility; and (4) allowing preemption here would improperly convert EPA’s registration process into broad tort immunity without clear congressional command.
key_precedents: Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. v. Albrecht (2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor rightly press that Wyeth and Albrecht caution against converting agency approval into tort immunity absent clear evidence the agency would have rejected the specific warning. But that rubric is tailored to implied impossibility in the FDCA setting; here § 136v(b) is an express preemption clause, and Bates makes the question whether the Missouri verdict imposes a non-parallel labeling “requirement … in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s. On this record, EPA’s repeated conclusions that a glyphosate cancer warning is not required and may be misleading mean the state-law verdict effectively compels label content that departs from the federally approved labeling judgment, undermining the uniformity Congress demanded, without our announcing any categorical bar to failure-to-warn claims. Justice Kavanaugh’s point that Albrecht confirms courts decide preemption supports keeping the holding narrow and fact-bound to this particular warning theory and this particular agency record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the hardest point that, absent a label-specific federal prohibition, Missouri’s failure-to-warn duty could be characterized as “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding standard under Bates, and that Wyeth/Albrecht’s “clear evidence” rubric should guard against converting federal approval into tort immunity. But Wyeth and Albrecht are implied-preemption cases; they cannot displace FIFRA’s enacted, express command in § 136v(b) that States “shall not impose” any labeling “requirements … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates already treats a common-law verdict as a “requirement.” As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the agency has repeatedly concluded a glyphosate cancer warning is not required and may be misleading; a state verdict compelling that warning necessarily imposes different label content than the federally administered baseline and thus falls outside Bates’s narrow parallel-duty safe harbor. Under an originalist/textualist approach, the statutory words—aimed at uniform labeling—control even if EPA’s communications are not styled as a formal ‘ban,’ because the state requirement still adds to or differs from the federal labeling requirements as actually administered.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that, under Bates and Wyeth/Albrecht, preemption should not attach absent clear, label-specific evidence that EPA would have rejected the particular cancer warning—so Missouri could be seen as enforcing FIFRA’s own misbranding standard rather than adding to it. But that approach imports an implied-impossibility framework into a case governed by FIFRA’s express command in § 136v(b) that States “shall not impose” labeling “requirements … in addition to or different from” federal ones, and Bates itself makes a tort verdict a “requirement” unless it truly runs in parallel with federal labeling duties. As the Chief Justice stresses, the practical effect of this verdict is to compel a glyphosate cancer warning that EPA has repeatedly deemed not required and potentially misleading; that is not simply “parallel enforcement” of FIFRA’s misbranding prohibition but a different label-content mandate that fractures the uniformity Congress demanded. Albrecht’s main relevance, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, is institutional (courts decide preemption) and does not negate the textual line § 136v(b) draws or the real-world compulsion created by the state verdict here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s strongest point is textual: § 136v(b) is an express uniformity rule and, under Bates, a jury verdict can be a state “requirement,” so the only safe harbor is a genuinely parallel duty. But I cannot accept Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s move from EPA’s repeated “not required/may be misleading” statements to a binding federal determination that the specific cancer-warning language Missouri supposedly compels is itself unlawful under FIFRA; that leap effectively turns registration and nonbinding risk assessments into tort immunity without the kind of clear, label-specific agency action Albrecht treats as legally operative. Justice Alito’s Mensing/Bartlett analogy also does not fit this statute’s design: FIFRA contemplates label amendments through EPA rather than a categorical federal bar on strengthening warnings, so a state failure-to-warn duty can still function as enforcing FIFRA’s own misbranding prohibition rather than adding a “different” requirement. Given the real-world consequences for injured plaintiffs and the absence of a concrete federal “no-warning” command on this record, I would treat the Missouri claim as plausibly parallel under Bates and therefore not expressly preempted.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I take the Chief Justice’s point seriously that § 136v(b) is an express uniformity rule and that, under Bates, a tort verdict counts as a state “requirement,” so Wyeth/Albrecht cannot simply be imported wholesale. But Bates’s safe harbor still turns on whether the state duty is genuinely “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding prohibition, and I do not think EPA’s repeated statements that a glyphosate cancer warning is “not required” and “may be misleading” (as Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize) amount, on this record, to a legally operative federal labeling requirement that affirmatively forbids the specific warning language the verdict would demand. Without a concrete federal command—e.g., a binding label disapproval or prohibition of that warning text—the Missouri duty can still be understood as enforcing the same bottom-line federal standard against misleading/inadequate labeling rather than imposing an “additional/different” requirement. Justice Barrett’s Mensing/Bartlett-style practical-impossibility framing is also less persuasive here because FIFRA contemplates seeking EPA approval for label changes, and absent clear, label-specific rejection, I cannot say the state duty necessarily compels “different” labeling in the sense § 136v(b) targets.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor rightly press that, under Bates, some failure-to-warn suits can be “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding standard and that Wyeth/Albrecht caution against turning agency approval into tort immunity absent “clear evidence” of rejection. But that “clear evidence” rubric is an implied-impossibility tool in a different statutory context and cannot displace FIFRA’s enacted, express line in § 136v(b): States may not impose labeling “requirements … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates confirms a jury verdict can be such a “requirement.” On this record—where EPA has repeatedly determined a glyphosate cancer warning is not required and has treated such warnings as potentially misleading—the Missouri verdict does not simply enforce FIFRA’s misbranding prohibition; it compels label content inconsistent with the federal labeling judgment, placing it on the “different from” side of § 136v(b) as Chief Justice Roberts explains. I would keep the holding narrow to this warning theory and this administrative record, but the text and Bates’s parallel-duty limit still support preemption here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor fairly press that, under Bates, a failure-to-warn verdict can be “parallel” to FIFRA misbranding, and that Wyeth/Albrecht warn against converting agency approval into tort immunity without clear evidence of rejection of the specific warning. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, this case turns on FIFRA’s express preemption in § 136v(b): the question is whether Missouri’s verdict, as applied, imposes a labeling “requirement” “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and EPA’s repeated determination that a glyphosate cancer warning is not required and may be misleading makes the state-imposed warning non-parallel to the federal baseline. Albrecht’s main contribution here is institutional—courts decide preemption—and it does not transplant Wyeth’s CBE-style “clear evidence” framework into a statute where Congress centralized label content and expressly barred divergent state labeling mandates. I remain for a narrow, record-bound preemption holding that targets this particular cancer-warning theory without announcing blanket tort immunity.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that Bates preserves “parallel” failure-to-warn claims and that, absent Wyeth/Albrecht-style clear evidence of rejection of the precise warning language, we should not treat EPA registration as tort immunity. But on a textualist reading, § 136v(b) turns on whether the state verdict imposes a labeling “requirement … in addition to or different from” the federal regime, and Bates itself makes a common-law verdict a “requirement” unless it genuinely tracks FIFRA’s misbranding standard. As Chief Justice Roberts frames it, EPA’s repeated determinations that a glyphosate cancer warning is not required and may be misleading within its labeling program make Missouri’s verdict functionally non-parallel—it compels affirmative label content the federal regulator has considered and declined, which is “different” for § 136v(b) purposes. Wyeth and Albrecht remain relevant to implied-preemption analysis, but they cannot displace FIFRA’s express preemption clause where the state duty, as applied, demands label language outside the federal labeling judgment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas press the strongest point: § 136v(b) is express preemption and, under Bates, a tort verdict can be a state “requirement” that is barred if it is non-parallel. But their conclusion still hinges on treating EPA’s repeated “not required/may be misleading” assessments as a legally operative federal requirement that forbids the specific cancer-warning language Missouri is said to compel; on this record, that looks more like a nonbinding regulatory position than a binding misbranding determination that would make the state duty “different from” FIFRA’s. Justice Alito’s Mensing/Bartlett analogy doesn’t persuade me because FIFRA’s scheme contemplates pursuing label amendments through EPA rather than categorically foreclosing strengthening warnings, so pragmatic conflict should be evaluated more like Wyeth/Albrecht’s focus on concrete, label-specific federal rejection. Given the consequences of converting routine EPA approvals into broad tort immunity without a clear, law-binding federal “no-warning” command, I continue to view the Missouri failure-to-warn theory as plausibly parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding standard under Bates.

John Roberts.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, common-law failure-to-warn duties can qualify as “requirements,” and they survive only if they are genuinely “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding standards; here, a Missouri verdict effectively compelling a cancer warning that EPA has repeatedly determined is not required (and, if misleading, would itself render the label misbranded) is not parallel but “in addition to or different from” the EPA-approved labeling regime. Given FIFRA’s centralized label-approval structure and the premise that Monsanto cannot unilaterally add the warning without EPA approval, the state-law duty operates as a conflicting labeling mandate, and a narrow ruling finding preemption on these facts best preserves federalism boundaries and institutional coherence without broader tort-immunity pronouncements.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: FIFRA’s text expressly preempts any state “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, common-law duties enforced through tort verdicts can constitute such “requirements,” and here the Missouri failure-to-warn judgment would effectively compel a cancer warning that EPA has determined is not required (and would therefore impose a non-parallel labeling obligation). Because FIFRA’s scheme makes EPA approval a prerequisite to label changes, the state-law duty—applied to mandate an additional warning contrary to EPA’s determination—conflicts with the federal labeling decision and falls within § 136v(b)’s preemptive scope.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and Bates held that common-law failure-to-warn verdicts function as such “requirements” because they set a standard the label allegedly violated. Here, EPA has repeatedly determined that a glyphosate cancer warning is not required (and may be misleading) and, under FIFRA’s approval scheme, Monsanto cannot unilaterally add such a warning without EPA approval, so the Missouri verdict would impose an additional or different labeling duty in conflict with the federally approved label. Unlike the “parallel requirements” carve-out in Bates, this state-law duty would not be “equivalent to, and fully consistent with” FIFRA’s misbranding regime because it would compel a warning EPA has affirmatively declined to require, creating a practical regime of 50-state labeling mandates that Congress sought to prevent through § 136v(b)’s “Uniformity.” Consistent with Mensing and Bartlett, when federal law withholds unilateral label-change authority and the state rule demands a different label, the state claim is preempted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FIFRA § 136v(b) preempts only state labeling “requirements” that are “in addition to or different from” federal ones, and Bates v. Dow allows state failure-to-warn duties to proceed when they are equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding prohibition against inadequate warnings. A Missouri verdict finding Roundup’s warning inadequate can be understood as enforcing that parallel duty rather than dictating a nonfederal label regime, especially where EPA registration and past risk assessments do not clearly amount to a binding federal prohibition on any cancer-warning language. Under Wyeth v. Levine and Merck v. Albrecht, impossibility preemption requires “clear evidence” the agency would have rejected the warning; Monsanto’s assertion that it could not change the label without prior EPA approval does not alone establish that a compliant warning was federally forbidden. Reading FIFRA to bar traditional tort remedies here would improperly convert EPA’s labeling process into near-immunity without the clear congressional statement § 136v(b) would demand, with the practical effect of foreclosing compensation and deterrence for seriously injured plaintiffs.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars only state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and Bates v. Dow Agrosciences instructs that common-law verdicts count as “requirements” but survive when they impose parallel duties equivalent to FIFRA’s own misbranding standard (e.g., labeling that is “false or misleading” or lacks necessary warnings). On this record, a Missouri failure-to-warn verdict can be understood as enforcing that parallel duty—requiring Monsanto not to sell an inadequately warned product—rather than dictating a particular label text that contradicts a specific EPA command. Unlike PLIVA v. Mensing and Bartlett, where federal law categorically barred unilateral label changes, FIFRA allows manufacturers to seek EPA-approved amendments, and Wyeth v. Levine cautions against treating agency approval as implied tort immunity absent “clear evidence” the agency would have rejected the warning; EPA’s general view that a cancer warning is “not required” is not necessarily a binding prohibition under § 136v(b) for preemption purposes. Given Bates’ narrow reading of § 136v(b) and the availability of a parallel-requirements framing, I would not find express preemption on these facts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause provides that a State “shall not impose or continue in effect any requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, common-law tort duties can constitute state “requirements,” and they survive only if they are genuinely “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding standards—not if they effectively demand a label change beyond what federal law requires. 544 U.S. 431, 443, 447 (2005). Here, the Missouri failure-to-warn verdict functions as a state-imposed labeling mandate to add a cancer warning that EPA has determined is not required (and has treated as potentially misleading), and because FIFRA’s scheme requires EPA approval before such a label change, the state verdict imposes an additional/different requirement barred by § 136v(b) and presents the kind of impossibility conflict recognized in PLIVA, Inc. v. Mensing and Mutual Pharmaceutical Co. v. Bartlett.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” those required under federal law. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, common-law failure-to-warn duties can constitute “requirements,” and are permissible only if they impose “parallel requirements” to FIFRA’s misbranding/labeling obligations. Here, a Missouri verdict effectively requiring Monsanto to add a cancer warning despite EPA’s contrary labeling determination is not parallel and would function as an additional state labeling requirement, and given the EPA-approval scheme for label changes, it also raises the kind of practical impossibility/conflict concerns recognized in Mensing and Bartlett (with the court, per Albrecht, assessing whether federal law actually permitted the change).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause bars any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, common-law failure-to-warn verdicts are “requirements for labeling,” and they survive only if they are genuinely “equivalent to, and fully consistent with,” FIFRA’s misbranding provisions; here, EPA has repeatedly determined that a glyphosate cancer warning is not required (and may be misleading), so Missouri’s verdict effectively imposes an additional/different labeling requirement. Given FIFRA’s regime that label changes require EPA approval, this case also resembles the impossibility/conflict logic of PLIVA, Inc. v. Mensing and Mutual Pharmaceutical Co. v. Bartlett, because the state-law duty would compel a label the federal regulator has rejected or not approved.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: FIFRA § 136v(b) preempts only state “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences a traditional failure-to-warn claim can survive if it operates as a parallel enforcement mechanism for FIFRA’s own misbranding standard rather than dictating novel, pesticide-specific label content. On this record, EPA registration and repeated approvals—without a formal, binding determination that a cancer warning is prohibited—do not clearly establish that Missouri’s verdict necessarily imposes a non-parallel labeling requirement, especially where state law is enforcing a general duty to provide adequate warnings against known risks. Consistent with Wyeth v. Levine, we should be reluctant to infer broad tort immunity absent a clear congressional command, and Monsanto’s impossibility argument is weakened where it could have sought EPA approval for strengthened warnings rather than treating the federal scheme as a categorical bar. Given FIFRA’s preservation of state authority in adjacent areas and the need for procedural fairness to injured plaintiffs, I would not find express preemption on these facts.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether FIFRA preempts a Missouri common-law failure-to-warn verdict demanding a glyphosate cancer warning that EPA has considered and determined is not required—and that Monsanto cannot add to the label without EPA approval.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA), 7 U.S.C. §§ 136–136y, especially the express preemption provision in § 136v(b) (states may not impose labeling/packaging requirements “in addition to or different from” FIFRA).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Monsanto argues that the state-law duty found by the Missouri courts is expressly preempted by FIFRA because it functions as a labeling “requirement” that is “in addition to or different from” EPA-approved labeling. Monsanto contends EPA has repeatedly evaluated glyphosate carcinogenicity and concluded a cancer warning is not warranted; moreover, FIFRA’s regulatory scheme bars Monsanto from unilaterally adding such a warning without prior EPA approval. Because the only way to satisfy the state-law duty is to change the federally regulated label in a way EPA has disallowed (or has not approved), the tort verdict effectively imposes a non-uniform, state-specific labeling mandate that FIFRA forbids. Monsanto also emphasizes a developed split among lower courts on how to apply FIFRA preemption when EPA has taken an affirmative position on the need (or lack thereof) for a particular warning.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Durnell argues that FIFRA does not preempt traditional state tort remedies that parallel FIFRA’s misbranding and adequate-warning standards, and that a state failure-to-warn claim is not automatically a forbidden “labeling requirement” merely because it may motivate a manufacturer to seek a label change. Respondent typically frames EPA registration and label approval as a floor, not a ceiling, and contends that EPA’s views about whether a warning is required do not necessarily amount to a binding federal prohibition on additional warnings. Durnell further maintains that Monsanto could have pursued available FIFRA mechanisms to add or modify warnings (or otherwise warn users) and thus cannot show the type of “impossibility” conflict needed to displace state law; in his view, allowing the verdict preserves states’ historic role in compensating injuries and deterring inadequate warnings.
key_precedents: Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, 544 U.S. 431 (2005)
Mutual Pharmaceutical Co. v. Bartlett, 570 U.S. 472 (2013)
Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. v. Albrecht, 587 U.S. 299 (2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest counterpoint: under Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht, EPA’s view that a cancer warning is “not required” may not equal a binding federal prohibition, so preemption should not attach absent clear evidence of rejection. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize, FIFRA supplies an express preemption rule—§ 136v(b)—and Bates makes the survival of state-law duties turn on whether they are genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding standard as implemented through EPA’s label-approval regime; a verdict that effectively compels a glyphosate cancer warning after EPA has repeatedly evaluated that precise question and approved labels without it is “different from” the federal labeling determination in operation and effect. Wyeth/Albrecht’s implied-preemption framework cannot override Congress’s text choosing national uniformity for pesticide labeling, particularly where the only practical compliance path is altering the EPA-approved label through EPA-controlled processes. A narrow opinion focused on this specific mismatch—rather than a broad tort-immunity rule—best addresses respondents’ federalism concerns while enforcing the statute and preserving institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is that Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht require “clear evidence” of a federal prohibition before preempting traditional tort remedies, and that EPA’s view a warning is “not required” is not the same as “forbidden.” But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, FIFRA contains an express preemption rule—§ 136v(b)—so the controlling textual question is whether Missouri has imposed a labeling “requirement … in addition to or different from” the federal scheme, not whether compliance is “impossible” under an implied-preemption framework. Under Bates, a tort verdict is a state “requirement,” and it survives only if it is genuinely parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding standard; where EPA has considered the carcinogenicity question and approved labeling without a cancer warning, a state duty compelling that warning is necessarily “different from” the federal labeling determination Congress made controlling. Wyeth/Albrecht therefore do not undermine the statutory-text analysis here, and I would adhere to preemption on the ground that the verdict operates as a nonuniform, state-specific label mandate barred by § 136v(b).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Wyeth/Albrecht point is the best counter: absent “clear evidence” EPA would have rejected the warning, we should hesitate to preempt traditional tort remedies. But that frames the case as implied impossibility preemption, while FIFRA supplies an express bar on state “requirements for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates makes clear a tort verdict counts as a “requirement” unless it is genuinely parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding standard. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, when EPA has repeatedly evaluated glyphosate carcinogenicity and approved labeling without a cancer warning, Missouri’s duty effectively compels a different label outcome, not merely parallel enforcement—precisely what § 136v(b) forbids. Albrecht does not displace that statutory text or authorize juries to impose non-uniform labeling mandates that contradict the federal label Congress made controlling.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the strongest point: that EPA repeatedly approved labels without a cancer warning, so a Missouri verdict effectively mandates a “different” label under §136v(b) and Bates. But Bates preserves common-law claims that parallel FIFRA’s misbranding/adequate-warning duty, and EPA’s determination that a warning is “not warranted” is not the same as a binding federal requirement that additional warnings would be false, misleading, or unlawful—especially absent the kind of definitive agency rejection Merck v. Albrecht treats as necessary to foreclose state remedies. Justice Alito’s Mensing/Bartlett analogy also does not fit because FIFRA does not impose the same “sameness” constraint and appears to allow registrants to seek label amendments, undermining the premise that the only lawful option was to keep the label unchanged. Given the statute’s savings structure and the real-world consequences for injured users who relied on the product’s warnings, I would not read §136v(b) to convert EPA approval into broad tort immunity without clearer federal foreclosing action.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest contrary point: under Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht, an agency’s view that a warning is “not required” is not necessarily a binding federal prohibition, and so tort law might operate as parallel enforcement. But that framing misfires in the FIFRA setting because §136v(b) expressly preempts state “requirements for labeling” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and Bates limits surviving common-law duties to those genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding standard as implemented through EPA’s label-approval process. As the Chief Justice emphasizes, where EPA has repeatedly considered the carcinogenicity question and approved a label without a cancer warning, a state verdict functionally compelling that warning is not “parallel” enforcement but a different labeling requirement in operation, which is what the text forbids. Albrecht’s clear-evidence inquiry matters for implied-preemption cases, but it cannot be used to dilute an express preemption clause that turns on whether the state duty would require a different label outcome than the federally approved one.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press that, under Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht, preemption should not attach absent “clear evidence” EPA would have rejected a cancer warning. But that framework addresses implied impossibility preemption; here Congress enacted an express bar in FIFRA: States may not impose “requirements for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements, and under Bates a common-law verdict is such a “requirement” unless it is genuinely parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding standard. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, where EPA has repeatedly considered the carcinogenicity question and approved labeling without the warning the jury effectively demands, the state duty does not merely enforce FIFRA’s standard—it yields a different label outcome, which §136v(b) forbids. The ability to petition EPA for amendments does not save the claim, because a state tort rule that pressures a registrant to obtain state-specific warning language still functions as a non-uniform labeling mandate contrary to the statute’s text and structure.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the best push under Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht: EPA’s view that a cancer warning is “not required” is not necessarily a binding federal prohibition, so tort law can sometimes operate as parallel enforcement. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, this case is governed first by FIFRA’s express text—§ 136v(b)—and Bates’s requirement that any surviving state duty be genuinely equivalent to FIFRA’s misbranding standard as implemented through EPA’s label-approval regime. A Missouri failure-to-warn verdict that, in practical effect, compels a glyphosate cancer warning after EPA has repeatedly evaluated that specific risk and approved labels without such a warning is not “parallel” enforcement; it functions as an additional/different state labeling requirement that Congress forbade to preserve national uniformity. Wyeth/Albrecht’s “clear evidence” framework for implied impossibility does not displace the statute’s express preemption rule here, particularly given FIFRA’s centralized control over label content and the resulting nonuniformity risk if juries can override EPA’s considered labeling judgments.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s best point is that Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht require “clear evidence” of a federal prohibition before displacing traditional tort remedies, and EPA’s view that a warning is “not required” may not alone establish impossibility. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas stress, this case is governed first by FIFRA’s express-preemption text—§136v(b)’s bar on any state “requirements for labeling … in addition to or different from” federal requirements—and Bates makes clear that a common-law verdict is a “requirement” unless it is genuinely parallel to FIFRA’s misbranding standard as implemented through EPA’s labeling determinations. Where EPA has repeatedly evaluated glyphosate carcinogenicity and approved a label without the cancer warning the jury found mandatory, the Missouri duty is not merely “parallel” enforcement; it demands a different label outcome and thus triggers the statute’s uniformity command without importing Albrecht’s implied-preemption framework. The respondent’s reading would effectively reduce §136v(b) to an impossibility test Congress did not write, allowing state-by-state labeling obligations that are “different from” the federally approved label in practical operation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the strongest point that §136v(b) is an express uniformity clause and, under Bates, a tort verdict can be a “requirement” that is preempted if it is “different from” the federal labeling outcome. But their approach effectively treats EPA’s registration decisions and repeated “not warranted” communications as the functional equivalent of a binding federal determination that adding a cancer warning would be unlawful, and that move is hard to square with Wyeth and Merck v. Albrecht’s insistence on clear agency action before we displace historic state remedies. Bates preserves state-law duties that parallel FIFRA’s misbranding/adequate-warning standard; a jury finding that this label was inadequate can be understood as enforcing that federal standard, not necessarily dictating specific label text, especially where FIFRA contemplates registrant-initiated amendment processes rather than a categorical unilateral-change bar like Mensing/Bartlett. Unless the record shows a definitive EPA rejection that would make compliance impossible or render the warning “false or misleading” under FIFRA, I would not read §136v(b) to extinguish this traditional damages claim.

John Roberts.reasoning: FIFRA expressly preempts any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences, common-law duties can be “requirements,” and they survive only if they are genuinely “equivalent to” FIFRA’s misbranding/adequate-warning standards rather than merely similar in the abstract. 544 U.S. 431, 443, 453–54 (2005). Here, because EPA has repeatedly considered glyphosate carcinogenicity and approved labels without a cancer warning—and Monsanto cannot unilaterally add that warning without EPA approval—the Missouri verdict functionally imposes an additional, non-federal labeling mandate that “diverges from” the federal scheme and is therefore preempted under § 136v(b).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: FIFRA expressly preempts any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), and this text covers common-law duties that operate as labeling mandates. Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, the question is whether the state-law duty is genuinely “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding standards; here, the Missouri verdict demands a specific glyphosate cancer warning despite EPA’s considered determination that such a warning is not required on the EPA-approved label, making the state duty “different from” the federal one. Because FIFRA’s scheme makes the EPA-approved label the governing label and the manufacturer cannot unilaterally add the state-required warning without EPA action, the verdict functions as a non-uniform state labeling requirement that § 136v(b) forbids. The Supremacy Clause requires giving effect to Congress’s chosen uniformity in pesticide labeling, even where state tort law traditionally operates.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause provides that a State “shall not impose or continue in effect any requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” those required under FIFRA. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences, common-law failure-to-warn duties qualify as “requirements for labeling,” and they survive only if they are genuinely “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding standards rather than imposing additional or different warnings. Here, the Missouri verdict effectively mandates a glyphosate cancer warning that EPA has considered and found not warranted, and because FIFRA requires EPA approval for label changes, the state-law duty operates as a non-uniform, extra warning requirement barred by § 136v(b) and akin to the impossibility concerns recognized in PLIVA v. Mensing and Bartlett when federal law prevents unilateral label changes.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FIFRA §136v(b) expressly preempts only state “requirements for labeling or packaging” that are “in addition to or different from” federal requirements, but under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences a common-law failure-to-warn verdict is not preempted when it enforces a parallel duty consistent with FIFRA’s misbranding/adequate-warning standards rather than dictating specific label text. EPA registration and label approval are important, yet they do not automatically amount to a binding federal prohibition on additional warnings for preemption purposes; as in Wyeth v. Levine and Merck Sharp & Dohme v. Albrecht, the manufacturer must show clear federal action making the state-law duty impossible to satisfy. Here, Monsanto’s argument depends on treating EPA’s view that a cancer warning is “not required” as categorically foreclosing state remedies, but FIFRA’s savings structure and Bates’ reading of §136v(b) preserve traditional tort compensation and deterrence where the claim can be understood as paralleling federal misbranding duties. Given the real-world stakes for injured users and the historic state role in providing remedies, I would not extend §136v(b) to wipe out the verdict absent a clearer federal prohibition.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: FIFRA expressly bars any state “requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” federal requirements. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences, a state tort verdict can constitute a “requirement,” and it escapes preemption only if it is genuinely “parallel” to FIFRA’s misbranding/adequate-warning standards; where EPA has affirmatively evaluated glyphosate carcinogenicity and determined a cancer warning is not warranted (and would risk being false or misleading), a Missouri duty to add that warning is not parallel but “different from” the federal determination. Given FIFRA’s scheme requiring EPA approval for labeling changes, this is not merely a state remedy operating alongside federal law, but a de facto state-specific label mandate that § 136v(b) forecloses.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause provides that a State “shall not impose … any requirements for labeling … in addition to or different from” those required under FIFRA. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences, common-law failure-to-warn duties are “requirements,” and they survive only if they are genuinely “parallel” to federal labeling obligations, not merely similar at a high level of generality. 544 U.S. 431, 443, 447, 453–54 (2005). Where EPA has evaluated glyphosate and approved labels without a cancer warning, and the only way to satisfy the Missouri verdict is to add a warning that would alter the EPA-approved label, the state-law duty necessarily imposes an additional/different labeling requirement and is therefore preempted under § 136v(b).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: FIFRA’s express “Uniformity” clause, 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b), bars any state-law labeling requirement “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s requirements, and Bates v. Dow makes clear that common-law failure-to-warn duties can qualify as “requirements for labeling,” while only truly “parallel” duties survive. Here, the Missouri verdict effectively demands a glyphosate cancer warning that EPA has considered and determined is not required on the EPA-approved label, so the state duty is not “equivalent to, and fully consistent with,” FIFRA’s misbranding scheme under Bates. Practical workability and judicial restraint also favor preemption: allowing juries to impose state-specific label standards despite EPA’s contrary labeling determination undermines FIFRA’s uniform federal regime and invites inconsistent nationwide labeling obligations. To the extent the question is framed as impossibility or “clear evidence,” cases like Merck v. Albrecht and PLIVA v. Mensing underscore that when federal law channels label changes through the agency and the agency has rejected (or would not approve) the warning, state-law liability cannot force a different label.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: FIFRA’s express preemption clause provides that a State “shall not impose or continue in effect any requirements for labeling or packaging in addition to or different from” those required under FIFRA. 7 U.S.C. § 136v(b). Under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences LLC, common-law failure-to-warn duties are “requirements” for labeling, and they survive only if they are genuinely “parallel” to FIFRA’s requirements rather than merely similar at a high level of generality. 544 U.S. 431, 443, 447, 453–454 (2005). Here, where EPA has evaluated glyphosate carcinogenicity and determined a cancer warning is not required on the approved label, a Missouri verdict demanding that very warning necessarily imposes a labeling requirement “in addition to or different from” the federal determination, frustrating FIFRA’s statutory command of uniformity and thus is expressly preempted.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 136v(b) preempts only state labeling “requirements” that are “in addition to or different from” FIFRA’s own misbranding/adequate-warning standards, and under Bates v. Dow Agrosciences a common-law failure-to-warn claim may proceed insofar as it functions as a parallel damages remedy for violating FIFRA-equivalent duties rather than creating a distinct state labeling regime. On this record, EPA’s registration and repeated statements that a glyphosate cancer warning is “not warranted” do not clearly amount to a binding federal prohibition that makes compliance with the state verdict impossible, especially given FIFRA’s mechanisms for seeking label amendments—so this looks closer to Wyeth v. Levine than to Mensing/Bartlett. Procedural fairness and practical consequences counsel against reading FIFRA to silently extinguish traditional state compensation remedies absent a clear congressional command or a clear “agency would not have approved” showing of the kind emphasized in Merck Sharp & Dohme v. Albrecht. Because the Missouri verdict can be understood as enforcing a duty to provide adequate warnings consistent with FIFRA’s misbranding standard rather than demanding a non-uniform label as such, I would find no preemption here.
